items._excerpt: Millar Western announced indefinite curtailment of Quesnel River Pulp. Millar Western Forest Products Ltd. will indefinitely curtail operations at its Quesnel River Pulp mill, citing market conditions and uncertainty surrounding economic fibre supply. The *Quesnel Cariboo Observer* obtained a copy of a letter sent out on Nov. 9, to employees at the Quesnel River Pulp mill. In the letter, executive chair and CEO Karl Meyers said the company had made the “very difficult decision” to curtail Quesnel River Pulp mill for an indefinite period. “Based on current contractual obligations, we will continue operating the effluent system for twelve months, or until we can reach an acceptable alternative,” Meyers said in the letter. “We will continue to complete an orderly shutdown of the balance of the operations over the next several weeks, setting it up for a potential restart in the future.” In August, Millar Western announced temporary curtailment of operations until at least November. Meyers said the company reviewed all alternatives before concluding that an indefinite curtailment was the only viable option at this time. According to the letter, the duration of the curtailment remains unknown and will depend on market conditions and the availability of economic fibre supply. “As a result, we will be terminating employment for all those impacted and providing severance compensation and other support,” Meyers wrote. He added the company will also provide continuation of certain benefits and access to employee and family assistance resources, with details to be outlined in individual severance letters. Meyers said Millar Western will also look at filling vacancies at other company operations with displaced employees. “For those who will continue to work, the period between now and your final day of employment will be considered as working notice,” he said. According to the letter, to qualify for severance, employees must remain active until their last scheduled day of work.

From spectators gathering for a flag-raising at a new Cenotaph in 1968 to veterans marching to city hall for a Korean War plaque dedication in 1994, Williams Lake has a long tradition of honouring those who served – one that continues. The Williams Lake and District Cenotaph was built in 1968 below the former War Memorial Hospital, a joint undertaking by the municipality and Royal Canadian Legion Branch 139 to honour the area’s war dead, according to the Veterans Affairs Canada’s website. The Cariboo War Memorial Hospital opened in May 1925, partly funded by the community of Soda Creek to honour fallen First World War soldiers. In 1968, the _Williams Lake Tribune_ reported on spectators gathering for a flag-raising ceremony at the new monument. Sixteen years later, the cenotaph was moved beside city hall and rededicated on Nov. 3, 1984, in conjunction with the dedication of the new municipal building. Days after the cenotaph’s rededication beside city hall, the _Tribune’s_ Nov. 8, 1984 edition outlined the plans for that year’s Remembrance Day Observance, bringing together veterans, students and community groups. The service began at 10:45 a.m. at the Elks Hall on Nov. 11, 1984 with the Williams Lake Community Band playing O Canada and a student from Anne Stevenson Junior Secondary School’s drama class reading In Flanders Field. Bill Lannigan and A.E McMath read the names of the former residents who died in the First and Second World Wars, followed by the Last Post and two minutes of silence. Smith’s family and community continue searching and are seeking government support for a coordinated operation with trained teams and equipment. Storms across southwestern British Columbia prompted rainfall warnings, with up to 250 millimetres forecast in parts of Vancouver Island. Flood watches remained in effect across much of the island and the south coast.

items.title: [cbc.ca] Parks Canada expects to eliminate about 500 full-time-equivalent positions, ends Banff rescue-dog program
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Parks Canada expects to eliminate about 500 full-time-equivalent positions, close 13 park-warden detachments and discontinue its Banff search-and-rescue dog program as part of $145 million in cuts over three years. The agency sent workforce-adjustment notices to 2,917 employees and says it will make individual decisions in the coming weeks. The Canadian Avalanche Rescue Dog Association and British Columbia Search Dog Association have urged the agency to reverse the cancellation, warning it could weaken rescue capacity. Parks Canada says it will shift wardens to a regional model focused on high-risk areas and that wardens can enforce park law without dogs. The associations say they are working on a short-term volunteer response during avalanche season.

The company improved the dirt roads and dug an electric-powered well, saving villagers a two-mile journey to fetch water from a cattle pond that often made them sick. It also gave dozens of local people forestry jobs.

“They fulfilled all their promises,” says Florencio Garcete, 55, chief of the Mbya Guaraní community of 211 people.

items.title: [cw39.com] Researchers favor permanent standard time as US debates clock changes
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Most U.S. clocks turn back one hour Nov. 1, as new research reviews renew debate over whether year-round standard time or daylight saving time better supports health. A Canadian policy analysis and a review focused on people with mental illness argue that permanent standard time better protects sleep, mood and biological rhythms. A broader review of population studies, however, finds a mix of harms and benefits from seasonal clock changes and summer daylight saving time. Permanent daylight saving time would delay winter sunrise, while permanent standard time would bring earlier summer sunrises and winter sunsets. The U.S. House passed a bill to make daylight saving time permanent in July 2026, but the Senate has not taken it up. The next seasonal clock change is scheduled for March 14, 2027.

items.content_html:

Cyberattacks disrupted refrigeration at grocery stores and other businesses in several European countries overnight into Nov. 2, raising temperatures in some units to 50°C and prompting businesses to discard food or remove it as a precaution. Affected countries included Belgium, Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia, Finland and Luxembourg; reports also described incidents in Italy, though the extent there remains unclear. In Belgium, Delhaize reported refrigeration problems in about 40 stores, Carrefour in 15 and Spar in five. Ireland’s SuperValu reported incidents at 13 stores, while refrigeration supplier Danfoss said at least 17 Dutch businesses were affected. The attackers appear to have remotely changed settings on connected equipment, in some cases activating defrost mode. European Agriculture and Food Commissioner Christophe Hansen described the repeated attacks as an attempt to disrupt food supply and weaken consumer trust, but said food security was not currently threatened. Belgian federal prosecutors opened an investigation, but no group has claimed responsibility and authorities have not established whether the incidents were part of one operation. Italy scheduled a government crisis meeting for Nov. 3 with national cybersecurity and intelligence officials.

items.title: [e.vnexpress.net] Travel technology provider Amadeus breach exposes 46,000 Singapore Airlines records
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Singapore Airlines said about 46,000 booking records may have been accessed in a breach at travel technology provider Amadeus, potentially exposing passenger names, booking references, itineraries and booking classes. About 620 records may also have included email addresses, phone numbers, travel-document details and KrisFlyer membership numbers. The airline said payment information was not exposed, bookings were not changed and its own systems were not breached. The unauthorized access involved booking data from August 2023 to September 2026. Cathay Pacific reported about 53,000 affected bookings, Japan Airlines about 92,000 affected customers and All Nippon Airways 37,800 affected records; Qantas is still checking whether its bookings were affected. Amadeus said it fixed the vulnerability and strengthened monitoring. Singapore Airlines is contacting customers with upcoming travel to change their booking references, while Singapore’s Personal Data Protection Commission said it is investigating.

items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

The European Commission convened two crisis meetings after cyberattacks on supermarket refrigeration systems spread across Europe, with incidents reported in at least 11 countries, including Germany and Romania. The attacks remotely raised temperatures or triggered defrost cycles, forcing retailers to discard food; no group has claimed responsibility, and authorities have not established whether the incidents share a perpetrator. The wave follows a similar attack on French supermarkets in October. A store in Lilienthal, Germany, said it had to discard goods worth more than €360,000, while six Romanian stores were affected. Italy’s government held talks with intelligence and cybersecurity officials and said the impact there was limited to a small number of commercial sites; it reported no health risk from thawed food. EU officials are coordinating with national authorities, who are conducting the investigations. Agriculture Commissioner Christophe Hansen said the bloc’s food supply was not currently threatened, and the Commission said the incidents showed a need for stronger cybersecurity across the EU.

El Niño-related peat fires and forest degradation in Southeast Asia are projected to push land-use carbon emissions higher in 2026, bringing total global CO₂ emissions to 43.3 billion tonnes even as fossil-fuel emissions edge down, according to the Global Carbon Project’s annual assessment. The researchers link the rise in land-use emissions to drier conditions and fires often ignited by human activity. The 21st Global Carbon Budget, published Nov. 10 in Earth System Science Data and presented during the U.N. climate conference in Antalya, projects 5.1 billion tonnes of emissions from land-use change this year. The projected decline in fossil-fuel emissions is partly attributable to the Iran conflict’s energy shock, alongside the growing contribution of solar, wind and electric vehicles. The report says the land carbon sink recovered in 2025 after weakening during the 2023-24 El Niño, but the strong 2026 El Niño is expected to weaken it again in 2027. Separately, an analysis of Chinese data found that emissions fell 3.1% in July-September, the country’s steepest quarterly drop since pandemic lockdowns in 2022.

The report’s 146 researchers from 30 countries urged governments to treat climate change as a global health emergency and coordinate a sustained response. Extreme rainfall affected 17.2% of global land each year from 2016 to 2025, up from 14.8% in the preceding decade, and the researchers linked shifting groundwater conditions to risks for food security and sanitation. Southeast Asia and Africa suffered the largest productivity-related economic losses, equivalent to 3.9% and 3.2% of gross domestic product, respectively. Clean-energy investment reached $2.1 trillion in 2025, nearly twice fossil-fuel investment, but fossil fuels still supplied more than 80% of global energy. The report calls for governments to consider health in climate decisions and direct climate and health funding to vulnerable countries. Researchers are expected to press the issue at the COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Türkiye, scheduled for Nov. 9-20.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists may have finally explained why our brains and bodies are cross-wired
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Scientists propose that the brain’s mysterious cross-wiring, which connects each hemisphere to the opposite side of the body, may have originated more than 500 million years ago in the visual systems of ancient fish. Rather than evolving for a specific advantage, this unusual arrangement may simply be a legacy of evolution building new brain circuits on an ancient foundation.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists discover metals that defy the deep freeze at -424°F
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Scientists have discovered a surprising mechanism that allows certain metals to resist cracking at temperatures as low as -253°C (-424°F), when similar materials typically become dangerously brittle. Instead of breaking, two experimental alloys reorganize their internal structures, creating new ways to absorb stress and remain flexible.

items.title: [ArchDaily] Reading the City from Above: Drone Imagery and the Material Layers of Urban Environments
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Beyond their buildings, infrastructure, and streets, cities can be understood as territories shaped by materials, resources, and processes of transformation that define their physical environments. As drone technology becomes increasingly integrated into architectural documentation and urban analysis, aerial imagery offers new opportunities to examine these different layers at multiple scales. As Jane Jacobs once suggested, "Cities are the mines of the future."
